questions.question: Give an overview of sorting algorithms in Java: bubble, insertion, merge, quicksort, heapsort. Cover time complexity, space complexity, and stability.
questions.title: Java Sorting Algorithms — Overview, Complexity, and Stability
questions.direct_answer: **Sorting algorithms** fall into two broad classes: **comparison-based** (O(n log n) lower bound) and **non-comparison** (O(n) for bounded-range integers). Java's `Arrays.sort` and `Collections.sort` use **TimSort** (for objects) or **Dual-Pivot Quicksort** (for primitives) under the hood. **Comparison-based sorts**: **Bubble sort** — O(n²) average and worst, O(1) space, **stable**, used only for teaching. **Insertion sort** — O(n²) worst, **O(n) on nearly-sorted**, O(1) space, **stable**, used for small subarrays inside hybrid sorts. **Merge sort** — O(n log n) all cases, O(n) space, **stable**, predictable, used for linked lists and external sorting. **Quicksort** — O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst (bad pivots), O(log n) stack space, **not stable**, fastest in practice for arrays due to cache locality. **Heapsort** — O(n log n) all cases, O(1) space, **not stable**, used when O(1) space is required and stability isn't needed. **Non-comparison sorts**: **Counting sort** — O(n + k) where k = range, stable, only for bounded integers. **Radix sort** — O(d · (n + b)) where d = digits, b = base; stable. **Bucket sort** — O(n + k) average; works when input is uniformly distributed. **Stability** matters when sorting by multiple keys (e.g., sort by name then by age — a stable sort preserves the first-key order within equal second-key groups). **Java's choice**: **TimSort** for objects (stable, adaptive, O(n log n) worst, O(n) for nearly-sorted) — best of all worlds for general use. **Dual-Pivot Quicksort** for primitives (no stability needed for int[], faster cache behavior). **For interviews**: know complexity, stability, and when each is preferred. Don't reinvent — use `Arrays.sort` / `Collections.sort` in production.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows time/space complexity of major sorting algorithms, the concept of stability, and Java's actual sort implementations (TimSort, Dual-Pivot Quicksort)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing average and worst case (quicksort O(n log n) avg vs O(n²) worst). Saying merge sort is O(1) space (it's O(n)). Forgetting non-comparison sorts. Not knowing TimSort is what Java uses
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention TimSort and Dual-Pivot Quicksort by name, discuss stability and when it matters, address O(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorts and how non-comparison breaks it, mention external sorting

sections.title: Sorting Algorithms — Complexity Cheat Sheet
sections.content:
| Algorithm | Best | Average | Worst | Space | Stable | Java use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bubble sort** | O(n) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | Yes | Teaching only |
| **Selection sort** | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | No | Rare; min-swaps |
| **Insertion sort** | O(n) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | Yes | Small subarrays in hybrid sorts |
| **Merge sort** | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n) | Yes | Linked lists, external sort |
| **Quicksort** | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n²) | O(log n) | No | Primitives in Java (Dual-Pivot) |
| **Heapsort** | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(1) | No | When O(1) space matters |
| **TimSort** | O(n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n) | Yes | **Java objects (Arrays.sort)** |
| **Counting sort** | O(n+k) | O(n+k) | O(n+k) | O(k) | Yes | Bounded-range integers |
| **Radix sort** | O(d(n+b)) | O(d(n+b)) | O(d(n+b)) | O(n+b) | Yes | Strings, integers |
| **Bucket sort** | O(n+k) | O(n+k) | O(n²) | O(n+k) | Yes | Uniformly distributed data |

sections.title: Comparison-Based Sorts — The O(n log n) Lower Bound
sections.content:
**Theorem**: any comparison-based sort requires Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. Proof via decision tree: with n! possible permutations, the tree depth is ≥ log₂(n!) ≈ n log₂ n.

**Bubble sort**: repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order elements. Easy to teach, never used in practice. Optimization: stop early if no swaps in a pass (best case O(n)).

**Selection sort**: find minimum, swap to front, repeat. Always O(n²). Notable for **minimum number of swaps** (n-1 swaps total), useful when writes are expensive (e.g., flash storage).

**Insertion sort**: build sorted prefix one element at a time. O(n) on nearly-sorted data — critical property used in hybrid sorts (TimSort, Introsort) for small subarrays. Stable.

**Merge sort**: divide-and-conquer; split, sort halves, merge. O(n log n) guaranteed. Requires O(n) auxiliary space. Stable. Best for **linked lists** (no array shifting) and **external sorting** (data larger than RAM).

**Quicksort**: pick pivot, partition (smaller / equal / larger), recurse. O(n log n) average; O(n²) worst (bad pivot — already-sorted with first-as-pivot). Mitigation: random pivot, median-of-three, dual-pivot. **Fastest in practice** for arrays due to cache locality and in-place partitioning.

**Heapsort**: build max-heap, repeatedly extract max. O(n log n) all cases, O(1) space. Slower in practice than quicksort due to cache-unfriendly heap structure.

**TimSort**: hybrid of merge sort + insertion sort. Detects existing 'runs' (already-sorted subsequences) and merges them. O(n) on already-sorted; O(n log n) worst. Stable. Java's default for object arrays since Java 7.

sections.title: Non-Comparison Sorts — Beating the O(n log n) Bound
Stability — Why It Matters
sections.content:
**Stable sort**: equal elements retain their **original relative order** after sorting.

**Example**: sort employees by salary; if two have same salary, the one added first stays first. Useful when:
- **Multi-key sort**: sort by primary key with stable algorithm; equal-primary entries retain secondary-key order.
- **Sequential sorts**: sort by name, then stably by age — result is sorted by age then name within age.
- **Database queries**: ORDER BY with multiple keys.

**Stable algorithms**: bubble, insertion, merge, TimSort, counting (if implemented carefully), radix.

**Unstable algorithms**: selection, quicksort, heapsort.

**Java's choice**:
- `Arrays.sort(Object[])` — **TimSort (stable)** — since Java 7.
- `Collections.sort(List)` — **TimSort** (delegates to Arrays.sort).
- `Arrays.sort(int[])` — **Dual-Pivot Quicksort** — not stable, but stability is meaningless for primitives (you can't tell two int 5's apart).
- `Arrays.parallelSort(...)` — parallel merge sort, **stable**.
- `Stream.sorted(...)` — stable.

**Trick**: if your algorithm is unstable but you need stability, augment elements with their original index and break ties by index.

**Production recommendation**: use `Arrays.sort` / `Collections.sort` — both stable for objects. For high-throughput primitive sorting, use `Arrays.sort(int[])` (Dual-Pivot Quicksort).

sections.title: Java Built-In Sort — What to Use
sections.content:
**Sort an int array** — Dual-Pivot Quicksort (fastest for primitives):
```java
int[] arr = {5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3};
Arrays.sort(arr);   // [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9]
```

**Sort a List<Integer>** — TimSort:
```java
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(5, 2, 8));
Collections.sort(list);   // [2, 5, 8]
// Or: list.sort(Comparator.naturalOrder());
```

**Sort with custom comparator**:
```java
List<Person> people = ...;
people.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getAge));
// Or descending:
people.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getAge).reversed());
// Or chained:
people.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getLastName)
                       .thenComparing(Person::getFirstName));
```

**Sort with parallelism**:
```java
Arrays.parallelSort(arr);   // parallel merge sort
```
- Uses ForkJoinPool.
- Worth it for arrays > ~8K elements.
- Stable for objects.

**Stream sort**:
```java
List<String> sorted = list.stream()
    .sorted()
    .toList();
```
- Returns a new sorted list; doesn't modify original.
- Stable.

**TreeMap / TreeSet**: maintain sorted order on insert, O(log n) per op. Don't 'sort' — just iterate in order.

**Don't write your own sort** unless: (a) you need a non-comparison sort for performance, (b) you need a special property (in-place external sort), or (c) it's an interview.

sections.title: Choosing the Right Sort
sections.content:
**Default for most cases**: `Arrays.sort` / `Collections.sort` (TimSort). Stable, O(n log n), adaptive (O(n) on nearly-sorted).

**Primitives, max speed**: `Arrays.sort(int[])` (Dual-Pivot Quicksort). Cache-friendly, no boxing.

**Parallel, large arrays**: `Arrays.parallelSort(...)`. Threshold ~8K elements.

**Need O(1) space**: heapsort. Rare in practice.

**Linked lists**: merge sort (no random access penalty).

**Bounded integer range**: counting sort — O(n + k).

**Integers / fixed-length strings**: radix sort.

**Uniformly distributed**: bucket sort.

**Data > RAM**: external merge sort.

**Already-mostly-sorted**: TimSort (best case O(n)).

**Need stability with custom comparator**: TimSort.

**Need top-K, not full sort**: heap (O(n log k)) or QuickSelect (O(n) average), not full sort.

**Need just min/max**: O(n) linear scan, not sort.

**Don't use bubble or selection sort in production** — ever. They're O(n²) with no compensating advantage.

**Don't write your own quicksort** unless you understand pivot selection and worst-case mitigation — it's easy to introduce O(n²) behavior.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Comparison-based lower bound**: Ω(n log n).
- **Non-comparison sorts** (counting, radix, bucket) achieve O(n) when applicable.
- **Bubble, selection, insertion**: O(n²). Insertion is O(n) on nearly-sorted, used in hybrids.
- **Merge sort**: O(n log n) guaranteed, O(n) space, stable, used for linked lists / external.
- **Quicksort**: O(n log n) avg, O(n²) worst, O(log n) stack, not stable, fastest for arrays.
- **Heapsort**: O(n log n) all, O(1) space, not stable, slower than quicksort in practice.
- **TimSort**: hybrid merge + insertion, stable, adaptive (O(n) on sorted), Java's choice for objects.
- **Dual-Pivot Quicksort**: Java's choice for primitive arrays.
- **Stability**: equal elements retain original order; matters for multi-key sorts.
- **Stable algorithms**: bubble, insertion, merge, TimSort, counting, radix.
- **Unstable**: selection, quicksort, heapsort.
- **Java APIs**: `Arrays.sort` (TimSort for objects, Dual-Pivot for primitives), `Collections.sort` (TimSort), `Arrays.parallelSort` (parallel merge), `Stream.sorted` (TimSort, returns new).
- **For multi-key sort**: use stable sort or `Comparator.comparing().thenComparing()`.
- **Trick to make sort stable**: pair with original index, break ties by index.
- **Don't use bubble or selection in production**.
- **Use built-in sorts unless you have a clear reason** to roll your own.
- **For top-K**: heap or QuickSelect, not full sort.
- **External sort**: data larger than RAM — chunk, sort each, k-way merge.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Sorting algorithms — two classes**

**Comparison-based**
- Lower bound: Ω(n log n)
- Bubble, insertion, selection: O(n²)
- Merge, quicksort, heapsort: O(n log n) average

**Non-comparison**
- Counting, radix, bucket: O(n) when applicable
- Don't compare pairwise; use value structure directly
- Beat the lower bound when range is bounded

**Major sorts**

**Bubble sort**
- O(n²) average and worst
- O(1) space, **stable**
- Teaching only; never in production

**Selection sort**
- O(n²) all cases
- O(1) space, **not stable**
- Notable: minimum swaps (n-1)

**Insertion sort**
- O(n) best (nearly-sorted), O(n²) worst
- O(1) space, **stable**
- Used in hybrid sorts for small subarrays

**Merge sort**
- O(n log n) guaranteed all cases
- O(n) space (auxiliary array)
- **Stable**
- Best for linked lists, external sort

**Quicksort**
- O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst (bad pivot)
- O(log n) stack space
- **Not stable**
- Fastest in practice for arrays (cache locality)
- Mitigations: random pivot, median-of-three, dual-pivot

**Heapsort**
- O(n log n) all cases
- O(1) space
- **Not stable**
- Slower than quicksort due to cache-unfriendly heap

**TimSort**
- Hybrid: merge sort + insertion sort
- Detects existing runs (sorted subsequences)
- O(n) on sorted, O(n log n) worst
- **Stable**
- **Java's default for object arrays since Java 7**

**Non-comparison sorts**

**Counting sort**
- O(n + k), k = range
- Stable
- Bounded integer keys (ages, grades)

**Radix sort**
- O(d · (n + b)), d = digits
- Stable
- Integers, fixed-length strings

**Bucket sort**
- O(n + k) average
- Uniformly distributed data

**Stability**

- Equal elements retain original relative order
- Matters for multi-key sorts
- Sort by name then stably by age → sorted by age then name within age

**Stable**
- Bubble, insertion, merge, TimSort, counting, radix

**Unstable**
- Selection, quicksort, heapsort

**Java's choice**

**TimSort for object arrays**
- Stable
- Adaptive (O(n) on sorted)
- O(n log n) worst
- Best of all worlds

**Dual-Pivot Quicksort for primitive arrays**
- Two pivots instead of one
- ~10-20% faster than single-pivot
- Stability irrelevant for primitives (can't tell two int 5's apart)

**Java APIs**

**`Arrays.sort(int[])`** — Dual-Pivot Quicksort

**`Arrays.sort(Object[])`** — TimSort

**`Collections.sort(List)`** — TimSort

**`Arrays.parallelSort(...)`** — parallel merge sort

**`Stream.sorted(...)`** — TimSort, returns new

**`TreeMap` / `TreeSet`** — maintains order on insert (red-black tree)

**Choosing the right sort**

**Default**: `Arrays.sort` / `Collections.sort` — TimSort

**Primitive max speed**: `Arrays.sort(int[])` — Dual-Pivot

**Parallel, large**: `Arrays.parallelSort(...)`

**O(1) space critical**: heapsort

**Linked lists**: merge sort

**Bounded ints**: counting sort

**Mostly sorted**: TimSort wins (O(n) best case)

**Top-K, not full sort**: heap (O(n log k)) or QuickSelect (O(n) avg)

**Just min/max**: O(n) scan, not sort

**Common mistakes**

**1. Confusing average and worst**
- Quicksort O(n log n) avg, O(n²) worst
- Merge sort O(n log n) ALL cases

**2. Saying merge sort is O(1) space**
- It's O(n) auxiliary

**3. Forgetting non-comparison sorts**
- Counting / radix can be O(n)

**4. Not knowing Java uses TimSort**
- For objects, since Java 7

**5. Reinventing sort**
- Use built-ins; they're well-tested

**Don't use in production**
- Bubble, selection — always worse than insertion

**Recommendation:** Always **use Java's built-in sorts** in production: `Arrays.sort` for objects (**TimSort** — stable, adaptive, O(n log n) worst, O(n) best case for nearly-sorted), `Arrays.sort(int[])` for primitives (**Dual-Pivot Quicksort** — fastest), `Arrays.parallelSort` for large arrays (parallel merge sort, threshold ~8K), `Collections.sort` (delegates to TimSort), or `Stream.sorted` (TimSort, returns new). For **interviews**, know the **complexity table cold** — best/average/worst time, space, and stability for each algorithm. Understand the **Ω(n log n) lower bound** for comparison sorts and how **non-comparison sorts** (counting, radix, bucket) break it for bounded-range integers. Know **why TimSort is Java's choice**: stable + adaptive + worst-case O(n log n) is hard to beat. Know **why Dual-Pivot Quicksort wins for primitives**: stability is meaningless, and the cache-friendly two-pivot partitioning is ~10-20% faster. Understand **stability**: it matters for multi-key sorts; use stable algorithms or augment with original index. For specialized scenarios: **merge sort** for linked lists and external sort; **heapsort** when O(1) space matters; **counting sort** for bounded integers; **radix sort** for fixed-length strings or integers; **bucket sort** for uniformly distributed data. **Don't use bubble or selection sort** in production — always worse than insertion. For **top-K**, use a heap or QuickSelect — don't full-sort. The mental model: **comparison sorts are bounded by O(n log n); structure-aware sorts can do O(n); Java's TimSort and Dual-Pivot Quicksort handle 99% of cases**.

questions.question: How do you sort a list of custom objects in Java? Cover Comparable, Comparator, and Comparator.comparing() with examples and chained ordering.
questions.title: Sorting Custom Objects in Java — Comparable, Comparator, Comparator.comparing()
questions.direct_answer: Java offers two main ways to sort custom objects: **(1) Implement `Comparable<T>`** — defines the **natural order** for the class via `compareTo`; used by `Arrays.sort(arr)` and `Collections.sort(list)` with no extra argument; one ordering per class. **(2) Pass a `Comparator<T>`** — defines an **external order**; used by `Arrays.sort(arr, cmp)` and `list.sort(cmp)`; multiple orderings per class. **Modern Java (8+)**: use **`Comparator.comparing(Person::getAge)`** factory methods for clean, type-safe comparators. Chain with **`.thenComparing(Person::getName)`** for multi-key sort. Reverse with **`.reversed()`**. **Implementing Comparable**: `class Person implements Comparable<Person> { public int compareTo(Person o) { return Integer.compare(this.age, o.age); } }`. **Implementing Comparator (lambda)**: `(a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.age, b.age)` — verbose; prefer `Comparator.comparingInt(Person::getAge)`. **For null handling**: `Comparator.nullsFirst(...)` / `nullsLast(...)`. **For descending**: `Comparator.reverseOrder()` or `.reversed()`. **Compare with Integer subtraction trick** (`a.age - b.age`) is **dangerous**: integer overflow if values are large opposite signs. Use `Integer.compare(a, b)` instead. **Chained comparison example**: sort by lastName ascending, then firstName ascending, then age descending: `Comparator.comparing(Person::getLastName).thenComparing(Person::getFirstName).thenComparing(Comparator.comparingInt(Person::getAge).reversed())`. **Stability**: TimSort (Java's default for object sort) is **stable** — equal elements retain their original order. Useful for multi-pass sorting. **Don't write `compareTo` that violates the contract** — must be **consistent with equals** (recommended), reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive. Buggy comparators (e.g., returning random values) cause `IllegalArgumentException` from TimSort.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows Comparable vs Comparator, can use Comparator.comparing() chains, handle null and reverse ordering, and avoid common bugs (subtraction overflow, contract violations)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `a.age - b.age` (overflow risk). Returning -1/0/1 inconsistently. Forgetting `.reversed()` is on the comparator, not the class. Mixing up Comparable's compareTo with Comparator's compare
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the Comparator.comparing chain idioms, address Integer.compare for overflow safety, mention TimSort stability, contract requirements (consistent with equals), and natural vs external ordering

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Comparable<T>**: defines natural order via `compareTo(other)`; one ordering per class.
- **Comparator<T>**: defines external order via `compare(a, b)`; multiple orderings per class.
- **`Comparator.comparing(extractor)`**: factory for type-safe comparators.
- **`Comparator.comparingInt/Long/Double`**: avoid boxing for primitive keys.
- **`.thenComparing(...)`**: chain for multi-key sort.
- **`.reversed()`**: reverse the ordering.
- **`Comparator.reverseOrder()`**: shorter for natural-order reversal.
- **`Comparator.nullsFirst/Last`**: null tolerance.
- **Use `Integer.compare(a, b)`** instead of `a - b` (overflow safety).
- **Comparable contract**: reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive; recommended consistency with equals.
- **TimSort throws** IllegalArgumentException on contract violations.
- **Java's `Collections.sort` is stable** (TimSort) — multi-pass sorting works.
- **For multiple orderings**: use Comparator, not multiple Comparables.
- **Common bugs**: integer overflow with subtraction, NPE on null, contract violations, modifying during sort.
- **Idiomatic Java 8+**: `list.sort(Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...))`.
- **`String.compareTo` is lexicographic**: 'A' < 'B' < ... < 'a' < 'b' (uppercase first).
- **Case-insensitive String sort**: `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER`.
- **TreeSet / TreeMap** use `compareTo` (or comparator) for membership, not `equals` — inconsistency causes bugs.
- **For complex sort logic**: chain comparators; if not expressible, write a custom lambda.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Two ways to sort custom objects**

**1. Comparable<T> — natural ordering**
- Class implements Comparable
- Override `compareTo(other)`
- Used by `Collections.sort(list)` with no extra arg
- One ordering per class
- For obvious natural order (Date, Integer, String)

**2. Comparator<T> — external ordering**
- Pass to `list.sort(comparator)` or `Collections.sort(list, comparator)`
- Multiple orderings per class
- Use for context-specific sorts
- Use for third-party classes you can't modify

**Java 8+ idiom — Comparator.comparing**

```java
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getName));
list.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Person::getAge));   // no boxing
```

**Chaining for multi-key sort**
```java
list.sort(
    Comparator.comparing(Person::getLastName)
              .thenComparing(Person::getFirstName)
              .thenComparingInt(Person::getAge)
);
```

**Reversing**
```java
Comparator.comparingInt(Person::getAge).reversed()
Comparator.comparing(Person::getName, Comparator.reverseOrder())
```

**Mixed direction**
```java
Comparator.comparing(Person::getName)
          .thenComparing(Comparator.comparingInt(Person::getAge).reversed())
```

**Null handling**
```java
Comparator.nullsFirst(Comparator.comparing(Person::getName))
Comparator.comparing(Person::getName, Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder()))
```

**Common bugs**

**1. Integer subtraction overflow**
- `a.value - b.value` overflows if values are extreme
- Use `Integer.compare(a.value, b.value)`
- Same for Long, Double, etc.

**2. Comparable contract violations**
- Must be reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive
- Recommended: consistent with equals
- TimSort throws IllegalArgumentException on violations

**3. .reversed() is on the Comparator**
- Not on the method reference
- `Comparator.comparingInt(Person::getAge).reversed()` ✔
- `Person::getAge.reversed()` ✘ (doesn't compile)

**4. compareTo vs compare confusion**
- Comparable.compareTo(other) — 1 param, this vs other
- Comparator.compare(a, b) — 2 params

**5. Null handling**
- Default comparators throw NPE on null
- Use nullsFirst / nullsLast

**6. Modifying during sort**
- Compared fields must be stable
- Concurrent modification → unpredictable

**7. Wrong primitive comparator**
- comparingInt avoids boxing
- comparing boxes int to Integer

**8. == vs .equals in compareTo**
- For Strings, use .compareTo() or .equals(), never ==

**Comparable contract**

- Reflexive: a.compareTo(a) == 0
- Antisymmetric: sgn(a.compareTo(b)) == -sgn(b.compareTo(a))
- Transitive: a > b and b > c implies a > c
- Recommended: consistent with equals (a.compareTo(b) == 0 iff a.equals(b))

**Stability — TimSort is stable**

- Equal elements retain original order
- Multi-pass sort works:
  - Sort by age first
  - Then sort by department — within department, age order preserved
- More common: chain comparators in one pass

**Real-world examples**

**Employees by salary desc, then name asc**
```java
employees.sort(
    Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary).reversed()
              .thenComparing(Employee::getName)
);
```

**Strings by length, then alphabetically**
```java
list.sort(
    Comparator.comparingInt(String::length)
              .thenComparing(Comparator.naturalOrder())
);
```

**Top 10 highest salary**
```java
employees.stream()
    .sorted(Comparator.comparingDouble(Employee::getSalary).reversed())
    .limit(10)
    .toList();
```

**TreeSet / TreeMap caveat**

- Use compareTo (or comparator) for membership, NOT equals
- If compareTo returns 0 for non-equal objects, they're treated as duplicates
- Inconsistency between compareTo and equals causes hard-to-find bugs
- E.g., HashSet with two equal-by-id but unequal-by-equals objects works fine; TreeSet treats them as one

**For interviews**
- Show Comparable for natural order
- Show Comparator.comparing chain for external
- Mention .thenComparing, .reversed, nullsFirst/Last
- Address Integer.compare for overflow safety
- Mention TimSort stability

**Recommendation:** Use **`Comparable<T>`** when your class has an **obvious universal natural ordering** (e.g., dates, numeric IDs); otherwise use **`Comparator<T>`** for **context-specific orderings**. The modern Java 8+ idiom is **`Comparator.comparing(extractor)`** with **`.thenComparing(...)`** for multi-key sort and **`.reversed()`** for descending; use **`comparingInt`/`comparingLong`/`comparingDouble`** to avoid boxing for primitive keys. Always use **`Integer.compare(a, b)`** instead of `a - b` to avoid integer overflow when values are extreme. For **null handling**, wrap with **`Comparator.nullsFirst(...)`** or **`Comparator.nullsLast(...)`**. The **Comparable contract** must be **reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive**, and ideally **consistent with `equals`** — inconsistency causes weird behavior in TreeSet/TreeMap. **TimSort** (Java's default for object sort) is **stable**, so multi-pass sorting works, but prefer chaining comparators in one pass. Avoid common bugs: **subtraction overflow**, **forgetting `.reversed()` is on Comparator**, **mixing up `compareTo` (one param) and `compare` (two params)**, and **modifying objects during sort**. The mental model: **Comparable = one natural order baked into the class; Comparator = pluggable orderings via factory + chain**. For **complex orderings**, build them declaratively with `Comparator.comparing(...).thenComparing(...).reversed()` — the chain reads top-to-bottom and is far cleaner than handwritten lambdas.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**TimSort** is a **hybrid stable sorting algorithm** combining **merge sort** and **insertion sort**, designed by Tim Peters for Python in 2002 and adopted by Java since version 7 for sorting object arrays (`Arrays.sort(Object[])`, `Collections.sort`).

It's **stable**, **adaptive** (exploits existing order in the input), runs in **O(n log n) worst case** and **O(n) on already-sorted data**, with **O(n) auxiliary space**. **Why Java uses it**: (1) **Stable** — essential for multi-key sorts and predictable behavior with custom comparators; (2) **Adaptive** — real-world data often has runs of sorted elements; TimSort exploits them; (3) **Worst-case O(n log n)** — unlike quicksort which can degrade to O(n²); (4) **Cache-friendly merging** — better performance than naive merge sort. **How it works**: (1) **Divide the array into 'runs'** — maximal sorted (or reverse-sorted) subsequences; reverse-sorted runs are flipped in place. (2) **Extend short runs to a 'minrun' length** (typically 32-64) using insertion sort — fast on small data. (3) **Merge runs** using a **stack-based strategy** that maintains invariants ensuring balanced merge sizes; uses **galloping mode** when one run consistently dominates the other (jumps ahead by exponential strides). **For primitive arrays** (`int[]`, `double[]`), Java uses **Dual-Pivot Quicksort** instead because stability is meaningless and primitive comparisons are cheap. **Performance**: ~O(n log n) typical; **O(n)** on already-sorted, reverse-sorted, or partially-sorted arrays.

Beats plain quicksort and merge sort on most real-world data. **Used by**: Java (`Arrays.sort`, `Collections.sort`, `Stream.sorted`), Python (`list.sort`, `sorted`), Android. **The standard answer** for 'why Java uses TimSort' is: stable + adaptive + O(n log n) worst case + better than quicksort/merge sort on real data.

A common mistake is confusing average and worst case (quicksort O(n log n) avg vs O(n²) worst). Saying merge sort is O(1) space (it's O(n)). Forgetting non-comparison sorts. Not knowing TimSort is what Java uses

sections.title: Comparable — Natural Ordering
Comparator — External Ordering
Comparable + Comparator Together
Common Bugs and Best Practices
sections.content:
**1. Integer subtraction overflow**
```java
// BAD: overflow if values have opposite extreme signs
return a.value - b.value;

// GOOD
return Integer.compare(a.value, b.value);
```
For `a.value = Integer.MAX_VALUE, b.value = -1`: `a - b = MAX_VALUE - (-1) = MAX_VALUE + 1` overflows to MIN_VALUE — wrong sign!

**2. Contract violations**
- `compareTo` returning random values → TimSort throws `IllegalArgumentException`.
- Inconsistent with `equals` causes weird behavior in TreeSet/TreeMap (which use compareTo, not equals, for membership).

**3. Forgetting `.reversed()` is on Comparator**
```java
// WRONG
people.sort(Person::getAge.reversed());   // doesn't compile

// RIGHT
people.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Person::getAge).reversed());
```

**4. Mixing up Comparable's compareTo and Comparator's compare**
- `Comparable.compareTo(other)` — single param, compares `this` to `other`.
- `Comparator.compare(a, b)` — two params, compares `a` to `b`.

**5. Forgetting null handling**
- Default comparators throw NPE on null.
- Use `Comparator.nullsFirst(...)` or `nullsLast(...)`.

**6. Modifying objects during sort**
- The compared fields must not change during sort.
- Concurrent modification → unpredictable behavior.

**7. Choosing wrong comparator for primitives**
- `Comparator.comparingInt(Person::getAge)` — no boxing.
- `Comparator.comparing(p -> p.getAge())` — boxes int to Integer; slower.

**8. Using `==` instead of `.equals` in compareTo for objects**
- `==` checks reference equality, not logical equality.
- For Strings: use `.compareTo()` or `.equals()`, never `==`.

**Best practices**:
- Use `Comparator.comparing(...)` factories.
- Chain with `.thenComparing(...)` for multi-key.
- Use `.reversed()` for descending.
- Use `Integer.compare`, `Double.compare`, etc., not subtraction.
- Implement `Comparable` only when there's an obvious natural order.

sections.title: Why Java Chose TimSort
sections.content:
Java pre-7 used **classical merge sort** for object arrays. Java 7 switched to **TimSort** because:

**1. Stability is essential for object sort**
- Multi-key sorting requires stable algorithms.
- Quicksort and heapsort are unstable; can't be safely used.
- Merge sort is stable but always O(n) auxiliary; TimSort is too, but better on real data.

**2. Real-world data has structure**
- Logs sorted by timestamp; mostly-sorted lists; concatenations of pre-sorted sublists.
- TimSort detects existing 'runs' and exploits them — O(n) on sorted, O(n log k) where k = number of runs.
- Plain merge sort always does O(n log n).

**3. Worst case O(n log n) guaranteed**
- Quicksort can degrade to O(n²) on adversarial input.
- TimSort never worse than O(n log n).

**4. Cache-friendly and low overhead**
- Galloping mode and bounded merge stack reduce comparisons and memory access.
- Beats classic merge sort and quicksort on most real benchmarks.

**Adopted from Python** — Tim Peters wrote it for Python's `list.sort` in 2002. Java borrowed it (with modifications) in JDK 7 (2011). Android's Java implementation also uses TimSort.

**For primitive arrays** (`int[]`, `double[]`, etc.), Java still uses **Dual-Pivot Quicksort**:
- Stability is meaningless (you can't tell two int 5's apart).
- Cache-friendly two-pivot partitioning is faster than TimSort for primitives.
- ~10-20% faster than single-pivot quicksort.

sections.title: TimSort Algorithm — Step by Step
sections.content:
**1. Find runs**: scan the array, identifying maximal sorted (ascending or strictly descending) subsequences.
- Ascending run: keep as-is.
- Strictly descending run: reverse in place (cheap O(k) for run of length k).
- Result: array partitioned into ascending runs.

**2. Extend short runs to minrun**: minrun is computed based on n (typically 32-64). If a run is shorter than minrun, extend it by inserting following elements via **binary insertion sort** (binary search for position, then shift).
- Insertion sort is fast on small subarrays (≤ 32) due to cache effects.
- Binary version reduces comparisons.

**3. Push runs onto a stack and merge**: use a stack of pending runs. After each new run, check stack invariants:
- For runs `A`, `B`, `C` at top of stack (A is bottom-most of these three):
  - **|A| > |B| + |C|**
  - **|B| > |C|**
- If invariants violate, merge `B` with the smaller of `A` and `C`. Repeat until invariants hold.
- This keeps merge sizes balanced; total merge work is O(n log n).

**4. Merge runs**: standard merge with two optimizations:
- **Galloping mode**: when one run wins consecutive comparisons (e.g., 7 in a row), jump ahead by exponential strides (1, 2, 4, 8, ...) using binary search. Speeds up merging when one run is much larger.
- **Bounded merge buffer**: copy the smaller run to temporary storage; merge in place.

**5. After all elements processed**: merge the remaining stack until one run remains — the sorted result.

**Complexity**:
- **Time**: O(n) best (already sorted), O(n log n) worst.
- **Space**: O(n) auxiliary (for merge buffer; effectively O(n/2)).
- **Stable**: yes — equal elements retain original order.

sections.title: TimSort vs Quicksort — Performance
sections.content:
| Property | TimSort | Quicksort | Dual-Pivot Quicksort |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Best case** | O(n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) |
| **Average** | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) |
| **Worst** | O(n log n) | O(n²) | O(n²) (rare) |
| **Space** | O(n) | O(log n) stack | O(log n) stack |
| **Stable** | Yes | No | No |
| **Adaptive** | Yes | No | No |
| **Cache-friendly** | Mostly | Yes (excellent) | Yes (better) |
| **Java use** | Object arrays | (Old; replaced) | Primitive arrays |

**Real-world performance**:
- **Mostly-sorted data**: TimSort wins big (O(n) vs O(n log n)).
- **Random data, primitives**: Dual-Pivot Quicksort wins (no overhead, cache-friendly).
- **Random data, objects**: TimSort competitive; comparison cost dominates anyway.
- **Stability required**: TimSort — only choice in Java's standard lib.

**Why Dual-Pivot Quicksort is faster for primitives**:
- Two pivots split into three regions: smaller, middle, larger.
- Reduces total comparisons by ~10-20% vs single pivot.
- Better cache locality.
- Stability irrelevant for primitives.

**Why TimSort wins for objects**:
- Object comparisons are expensive (virtual call to `compareTo`).
- Adaptive nature reduces comparisons on real data.
- Stability required for many use cases.
- Merge phase amortizes comparison cost.

sections.title: Galloping Mode — The Speedup Trick
sections.content:
**Standard merge** of two runs: compare heads, take smaller, advance. O(n) per merge.

**Problem**: if one run is much larger or one consistently wins, you waste comparisons. Example merging `[1, 2, 3]` and `[100, 200, 300]`: every comparison is trivially won by run 1; we do 3 comparisons just to copy [1, 2, 3].

**Galloping**: when one run wins **MIN_GALLOP** (typically 7) consecutive comparisons, switch to galloping mode:
- **Binary search** for the winning run's largest value ≤ the losing run's head.
- Bulk-copy that range from the winning run.
- Resume normal mode.

**Effect**:
- For consistently dominant runs, merge is O(log n) per 'gallop' instead of O(n) total comparisons.
- Significantly speeds up merging of pre-sorted concatenations.

**Adaptive threshold**:
- If galloping pays off, decrease MIN_GALLOP — enter galloping sooner.
- If galloping wastes work (false signals), increase MIN_GALLOP.
- This adaptation responds to data structure dynamically.

**The merge-stack invariants**:
- Tim's algorithm maintains a stack of pending runs.
- Invariants ensure that each run is merged with one of similar size, so total work is O(n log n).
- A 2018 paper found a subtle bug in the original invariants for very large arrays — fixed in subsequent JDK releases.

**Edge cases to know**:
- TimSort throws `IllegalArgumentException` if the comparator violates the contract (detected during merge).
- Performance degrades to O(n log n) — not catastrophic — if the data has no exploitable structure.

sections.title: When TimSort Excels and When It Doesn't
sections.content:
**TimSort excels on**:
- **Already-sorted or reverse-sorted data**: O(n) best case.
- **Partially-sorted data** with long runs: O(n) on the runs + O(n log k) merging where k = number of runs.
- **Concatenations of sorted sublists**: detects each as a run.
- **Object arrays**: stability + adaptive nature + manageable comparison count.
- **Real-world data**: most production data has structure; TimSort exploits it.

**TimSort doesn't shine on**:
- **Random primitive arrays**: Dual-Pivot Quicksort is faster (cheaper comparisons, better cache).
- **Memory-constrained**: O(n) auxiliary may be a problem; heapsort offers O(1) space.
- **Pathological adversarial input**: O(n log n) but constants higher than quicksort on truly random data.

**Java's smart split**:
- `Arrays.sort(int[])` → Dual-Pivot Quicksort.
- `Arrays.sort(Object[])` → TimSort.
- `Arrays.parallelSort(...)` → parallel merge sort (also stable).
- `Stream.sorted(...)` → TimSort.
- `Collections.sort` → delegates to `List.sort` which uses TimSort.

**You don't need to choose** — Java picks the right algorithm based on the input type. Just use the standard APIs.

**Production tip**: don't write your own sort. The JDK implementations are extensively tested, optimized, and patched. Reinventing them is a waste.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **TimSort**: hybrid sort combining merge sort + insertion sort.
- **Used by**: Java (`Arrays.sort(Object[])`, `Collections.sort`, `Stream.sorted`), Python, Android.
- **Stable**: equal elements retain original order — essential for multi-key sorts.
- **Adaptive**: O(n) on sorted/reverse-sorted, O(n log k) for k runs.
- **Worst case O(n log n)** — never degrades to O(n²) like quicksort.
- **Space**: O(n) auxiliary for merge buffer.
- **Algorithm steps**: find runs → extend to minrun via insertion sort → merge with stack invariants → use galloping mode for dominant runs.
- **Minrun**: typically 32-64; insertion sort fast on small subarrays.
- **Galloping mode**: binary search to skip ahead when one run dominates.
- **Merge stack invariants**: keep merges balanced; ensure O(n log n).
- **For primitive arrays**: Java uses **Dual-Pivot Quicksort** (faster, stability irrelevant).
- **Why Java chose TimSort for objects**: stable + adaptive + O(n log n) worst case + reduces comparisons.
- **Comparison cost matters**: object comparisons (virtual calls to compareTo) are expensive; TimSort minimizes them.
- **Adopted from Python**: Tim Peters' design from 2002.
- **Throws IllegalArgumentException** on contract violations in comparator.
- **For interviews**: know it's Java's default for objects, mention adaptive behavior, runs, galloping, and contrast with Dual-Pivot for primitives.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**TimSort** is a **hybrid sorting algorithm** combining merge sort and insertion sort. It's **Java's default for sorting object arrays** since Java 7.

**Key properties**
- **Stable**: equal elements retain original order
- **Adaptive**: O(n) on already-sorted, O(n log k) for k runs
- **Worst case O(n log n)** — never O(n²)
- **Space**: O(n) auxiliary

**Why Java chose it for objects**

**1. Stability essential**
- Multi-key sorts need it
- Quicksort/heapsort unstable
- Predictable behavior for custom comparators

**2. Adaptive on real data**
- Real data often has structure (timestamps, IDs)
- TimSort detects sorted runs and exploits them
- Best case O(n)

**3. Worst case O(n log n)**
- Quicksort can degrade to O(n²)
- TimSort always O(n log n)

**4. Reduces comparisons**
- Object comparisons are expensive (virtual call to compareTo)
- Adaptive nature minimizes them

**Algorithm steps**

**1. Find runs**
- Scan for maximal sorted (or strictly descending) subsequences
- Reverse descending runs in place
- Result: array partitioned into ascending runs

**2. Extend short runs to minrun**
- minrun = 32-64 typically
- Use binary insertion sort for short runs (fast on small data)
- Insertion sort exploits cache locality

**3. Push runs onto stack, merge with invariants**
- Stack of pending runs
- Invariants: |A| > |B| + |C|, |B| > |C|
- If violated, merge B with smaller of A and C
- Keeps merges balanced — total O(n log n)

**4. Merge with galloping mode**
- Standard merge: compare heads
- After 7 consecutive wins by one side: switch to galloping
- Binary search to skip ahead, bulk-copy
- Speeds up merging when one run dominates

**Galloping example**
- Merging [1,2,3] and [100,200,300]
- Without galloping: 3 comparisons all trivially won by run 1
- With galloping: binary search; bulk copy [1,2,3]; done in O(log n)

**Adaptive threshold**
- If galloping pays off, lower threshold (gallop sooner)
- If wasted, raise threshold
- Self-tunes to data

**Performance comparison**

**TimSort**
- Best O(n)
- Average O(n log n)
- Worst O(n log n)
- Space O(n)
- Stable, adaptive

**Plain quicksort**
- Best/average O(n log n)
- Worst O(n²)
- Space O(log n)
- Not stable, not adaptive

**Dual-pivot quicksort (Java's primitive sort)**
- Best/average O(n log n)
- Worst O(n²) but very rare
- Space O(log n)
- Not stable, not adaptive
- ~10-20% faster than single-pivot for primitives

**Why Java splits**

**Object arrays → TimSort**
- Stability matters
- Comparison cost dominates
- Adaptive on real data

**Primitive arrays → Dual-Pivot Quicksort**
- Stability meaningless (can't tell two int 5's apart)
- Cheap comparisons
- Better cache locality

**Other Java sort APIs**

- `Arrays.sort(Object[])` — TimSort
- `Arrays.sort(int[])` — Dual-Pivot Quicksort
- `Arrays.parallelSort(...)` — parallel merge sort (stable)
- `Collections.sort` — delegates to List.sort → TimSort
- `Stream.sorted(...)` — TimSort, returns new stream
- `TreeMap` / `TreeSet` — red-black tree, sorted on insert (not 'sort')

**TimSort excels on**
- Already sorted / reverse sorted (O(n))
- Partially sorted (long runs)
- Concatenations of sorted sublists
- Object arrays
- Real-world structured data

**Doesn't excel**
- Random primitive arrays (Dual-Pivot wins)
- Memory-constrained (O(n) aux)
- Pure random data with cheap comparisons

**Bug history (interesting)**
- 2018 paper found subtle issue with merge stack invariants for huge arrays
- Fixed in subsequent JDK releases
- Algorithm has been battle-tested over 20+ years

**Adopted from Python**
- Tim Peters wrote it in 2002
- Java borrowed in JDK 7 (2011)
- Android also uses it

**Recommendation:** Java uses **TimSort** for **object arrays** (`Arrays.sort(Object[])`, `Collections.sort`, `Stream.sorted`) because it's **stable** (essential for multi-key sorts), **adaptive** (O(n) on sorted/reverse-sorted, exploits real-world structure), has **worst-case O(n log n)** (unlike quicksort), and **minimizes expensive object comparisons**. For **primitive arrays**, Java uses **Dual-Pivot Quicksort** because stability is meaningless (you can't distinguish two int 5's), comparisons are cheap, and the cache-friendly two-pivot partitioning is ~10-20% faster than single-pivot quicksort. **TimSort's algorithm**: (1) find runs (maximal sorted/reverse-sorted subsequences); (2) extend short runs to **minrun** (32-64) via binary insertion sort (fast on small data); (3) merge runs using a **stack-based strategy** with invariants that keep merge sizes balanced; (4) use **galloping mode** to skip ahead when one run dominates (binary-search + bulk-copy). The algorithm is **adopted from Python** (Tim Peters, 2002) and used by Java since version 7 and Android. **Don't reinvent it** — always use Java's built-in sort APIs; they're extensively tested, well-optimized, and patched for edge cases. The mental model: **TimSort = merge sort that's smart about real-world structure**; on already-sorted data it's linear, on adversarial input it's still O(n log n) — best of both worlds for general object sorting.

questions.question: How do you implement binary search in Java? Cover iterative and recursive versions, and the correct use of `Collections.binarySearch()`.
questions.title: Binary Search in Java — Iterative, Recursive, and Collections.binarySearch()
questions.direct_answer: **Binary search** finds a target in a **sorted** array/list in **O(log n)** time by repeatedly halving the search range. Three implementations: **(1) Iterative** (preferred): `low = 0, high = n - 1; while (low <= high) { mid = low + (high - low) / 2; ... }`. O(log n) time, O(1) space. **(2) Recursive**: similar logic with recursion. O(log n) time, **O(log n) stack space**. **(3) `Collections.binarySearch(list, key)`** or **`Arrays.binarySearch(arr, key)`** — JDK's built-in, returns the index if found, or `-(insertion_point) - 1` if not found. **Critical bugs to avoid**: (1) `(low + high) / 2` can **overflow** if `low + high > Integer.MAX_VALUE`; use `low + (high - low) / 2` instead. (2) Wrong loop condition (`low < high` vs `low <= high`) misses or skips elements. (3) Wrong update (`high = mid` vs `high = mid - 1`) causes infinite loops or off-by-one. **Variants**: **lower bound** (first index >= target), **upper bound** (first index > target), **search range** [first occurrence, last occurrence], **search in rotated sorted array**, **search in 2D matrix**, **find peak element**, **find min in rotated array**. **`Collections.binarySearch`** requires either natural ordering (Comparable) or a Comparator; the list must be sorted. **Returns**: index if found; `-(insertion_point) - 1` if not. To compute insertion point: `int ip = -result - 1` if not found. **Edge cases**: empty array, single element, target at boundaries, duplicates (binary search returns any matching index, not necessarily first or last — use lower/upper bound for those). **Don't use binary search on unsorted arrays** — sort first (O(n log n)) only if amortized over many searches; otherwise linear scan is O(n).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Binary search**: O(log n) time, O(1) iterative or O(log n) recursive.
- **Requires sorted input**.
- **Avoid overflow**: `low + (high - low) / 2`, not `(low + high) / 2`.
- **Loop condition** `low <= high` for standard search; `low < high` for lower/upper bound.
- **Update with `mid + 1` / `mid - 1`** to make progress and avoid infinite loops.
- **`Collections.binarySearch` / `Arrays.binarySearch`**: returns index or `-(insertion_point) - 1`.
- **Insertion point**: `result >= 0 ? result : -result - 1`.
- **For duplicates**: standard binary search returns any match — use lower/upper bound for first/last.
- **Lower bound**: first index `>= target`.
- **Upper bound**: first index `> target`.
- **Range count**: `upperBound - lowerBound`.
- **Rotated sorted array search**: O(log n) by determining which half is sorted.
- **2D matrix search**: O(m + n) walking from top-right.
- **Peak element**: O(log n) following the gradient.
- **Common bugs**: overflow, off-by-one, wrong loop condition, infinite loop with `low = mid`.
- **Don't use binary search on unsorted data** — results undefined.
- **For LinkedList**: don't use `Collections.binarySearch` — O(n) due to traversal.
- **`TreeMap` / `TreeSet`**: maintain sorted order; `ceilingKey`/`floorKey` give bound queries in O(log n).
- **Generalize**: 'binary search the answer' applies to monotone problems (find smallest x satisfying P(x)).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Binary search** finds a target in a **sorted** array in **O(log n)** time by repeatedly halving the search range.

**Standard iterative version**
```java
low = 0, high = n - 1
while (low <= high) {
    mid = low + (high - low) / 2
    if arr[mid] == target: return mid
    if arr[mid] < target: low = mid + 1
    else: high = mid - 1
}
return -1
```

**Critical correctness points**

**1. Overflow-safe mid**
- `(low + high) / 2` overflows if low + high > Integer.MAX_VALUE
- Use `low + (high - low) / 2`
- Famous JDK bug fixed in 2006

**2. Loop condition**
- `low <= high` — search range non-empty
- `low < high` — wrong; misses cases when low == high

**3. Updates**
- `low = mid + 1` (not low = mid)
- `high = mid - 1` (not high = mid)
- We've checked arr[mid] != target; skip it
- Without +1/-1: infinite loop when high = low + 1

**Recursive version**
- Same logic with recursion
- O(log n) stack space
- log₂(2^31) ≈ 31 — safe stack depth
- Iterative is just as clean; rare to choose recursive

**Variants**

**Lower bound (first index >= target)**
- high = n (not n-1)
- `low < high` (strict)
- `high = mid` (not mid - 1)
- Returns insertion point preserving sort order
- Useful for first occurrence, count of elements < target

**Upper bound (first index > target)**
- Similar; `arr[mid] <= target` advances low
- For last occurrence (subtract 1), count elements <= target

**Range count**
- count = upperBound(target) - lowerBound(target)
- Handles duplicates

**Java built-ins**

**Arrays.binarySearch / Collections.binarySearch**
- Requires sorted input
- Returns index if found
- Returns `-(insertion_point) - 1` if not found
- For not-found: `int ip = -result - 1`

**Caveats**
- Doesn't return first/last for duplicates — just any match
- Use lower/upper bound for those
- LinkedList: O(n) due to traversal — don't use

**With Comparator**
- `Collections.binarySearch(list, key, comparator)`
- Comparator must match the sort order

**Complex variants**

**Search in rotated sorted array**
- O(log n)
- Determine which half is sorted
- Check if target is in that half

**2D matrix search (sorted rows + cols)**
- Walk from top-right
- Down if too small, left if too large
- O(m + n)

**Find peak element**
- Compare mid to mid+1
- Follow the gradient up
- O(log n)

**Find min in rotated sorted array**
- Compare mid to high
- O(log n)

**Binary search the answer**
- For monotone problems (find smallest x satisfying P(x))
- Examples: square root, capacity to ship, K-th smallest
- Search the answer space, not the array

**Common bugs**

**1. Overflow**
- (low + high) / 2 can overflow
- Use low + (high - low) / 2

**2. Off-by-one**
- Wrong loop condition
- Wrong updates (mid vs mid+1)
- Drawing the search range helps

**3. Infinite loop**
- `low = mid` without +1
- When high = low + 1, mid = low, no progress

**4. Using on unsorted data**
- Results undefined
- Sort first or use linear scan

**5. Misunderstanding negative return**
- Collections.binarySearch returns -(ip+1)
- Not -1; not 0
- ip = -result - 1

**6. Wrong comparator**
- Must match the sort order used
- Inconsistent comparator → wrong results

**Performance**

- Binary search: O(log n)
- Linear scan: O(n)
- Sort then binary search: O(n log n) — only worth it if many searches amortize the sort
- TreeMap / TreeSet: O(log n) per operation, no sort needed (always sorted)

**For interviews**

**Standard binary search**
- Iterative version
- Overflow-safe mid
- Correct loop condition and updates

**Lower / upper bound**
- For first/last occurrence with duplicates
- For range counts

**Variants**
- Rotated sorted, 2D matrix, peak, find min
- 'Binary search the answer' for monotone problems

**Java APIs**
- Arrays.binarySearch / Collections.binarySearch
- Insertion point convention

**Recommendation:** For **binary search**, always use the **iterative version** with the **overflow-safe mid**: `int mid = low + (high - low) / 2` — the famous `(low + high) / 2` overflow bug went undetected in Java's standard library for ~9 years. Use **`low <= high`** for the loop condition and **`mid + 1` / `mid - 1`** for updates to ensure progress and avoid infinite loops. For **first or last occurrence with duplicates**, use **lower bound** (first index `>= target`) or **upper bound** (first index `> target`) variants — these have slightly different invariants (`high = n`, `low < high`, `high = mid`). For **Java's built-ins** (`Arrays.binarySearch`, `Collections.binarySearch`), remember the **insertion-point convention**: returns `-(insertion_point) - 1` if not found; compute `int ip = -result - 1`. Don't use `Collections.binarySearch` on a **LinkedList** (O(n) traversal cost). Know the **classic variants**: search in rotated sorted array (O(log n) by determining which half is sorted), 2D matrix search (O(m+n) walking from top-right), find peak element (O(log n) following gradient), and **'binary search the answer'** for monotone problems (square root, capacity-to-ship, K-th smallest). For **sorted maps/sets**, prefer **`TreeMap.ceilingKey/floorKey`** over manual binary search — same O(log n) but more idiomatic. Always verify the **input is sorted**; binary search on unsorted data has undefined behavior. The mental model: **binary search = halve the range each step using a comparison**; if the comparison gives monotone information about where the answer can be, it works — not just for arrays but for any monotone search space.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
**TimSort** is a **hybrid stable sorting algorithm** combining **merge sort** and **insertion sort**, designed by Tim Peters for Python in 2002 and adopted by Java since version 7 for sorting object arrays (`Arrays.sort(Object[])`, `Collections.sort`).

It's **stable**, **adaptive** (exploits existing order in the input), runs in **O(n log n) worst case** and **O(n) on already-sorted data**, with **O(n) auxiliary space**. **Why Java uses it**: (1) **Stable** — essential for multi-key sorts and predictable behavior with custom comparators; (2) **Adaptive** — real-world data often has runs of sorted elements; TimSort exploits them; (3) **Worst-case O(n log n)** — unlike quicksort which can degrade to O(n²); (4) **Cache-friendly merging** — better performance than naive merge sort. **How it works**: (1) **Divide the array into 'runs'** — maximal sorted (or reverse-sorted) subsequences; reverse-sorted runs are flipped in place. (2) **Extend short runs to a 'minrun' length** (typically 32-64) using insertion sort — fast on small data. (3) **Merge runs** using a **stack-based strategy** that maintains invariants ensuring balanced merge sizes; uses **galloping mode** when one run consistently dominates the other (jumps ahead by exponential strides). **For primitive arrays** (`int[]`, `double[]`), Java uses **Dual-Pivot Quicksort** instead because stability is meaningless and primitive comparisons are cheap. **Performance**: ~O(n log n) typical; **O(n)** on already-sorted, reverse-sorted, or partially-sorted arrays.

Beats plain quicksort and merge sort on most real-world data. **Used by**: Java (`Arrays.sort`, `Collections.sort`, `Stream.sorted`), Python (`list.sort`, `sorted`), Android. **The standard answer** for 'why Java uses TimSort' is: stable + adaptive + O(n log n) worst case + better than quicksort/merge sort on real data.

A common mistake is confusing average and worst case (quicksort O(n log n) avg vs O(n²) worst). Saying merge sort is O(1) space (it's O(n)). Forgetting non-comparison sorts. Not knowing TimSort is what Java uses

sections.title: Iterative Binary Search — The Standard
sections.content:
```java
public int binarySearch(int[] arr, int target) {
    int low = 0, high = arr.length - 1;
    while (low <= high) {
        int mid = low + (high - low) / 2;   // overflow-safe
        if (arr[mid] == target) return mid;
        if (arr[mid] < target) low = mid + 1;
        else high = mid - 1;
    }
    return -1;   // not found
}
```

**Why `low + (high - low) / 2`?**
- `(low + high) / 2` can **overflow** if `low + high > Integer.MAX_VALUE` (e.g., low=high=2 billion).
- `low + (high - low) / 2` is mathematically equivalent and overflow-safe.
- This bug famously existed in the JDK's `Arrays.binarySearch` for ~9 years until Joshua Bloch's blog post in 2006.

**Why `low <= high`?**
- Loop continues as long as the search range is non-empty.
- When low > high, range is empty — target not found.

**Why `mid + 1` and `mid - 1`?**
- We've already checked `arr[mid] != target`.
- Skip mid in next iteration to make progress.
- `low = mid` (without +1) can cause infinite loop when high = low + 1.

**Complexity**: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

**Edge cases**:
- Empty array: high = -1; loop doesn't execute; return -1.
- Single element matching: low = high = 0, mid = 0, return 0.
- Single element not matching: loop runs once, return -1.
- Target at boundaries: handled by mid + 1 / mid - 1 updates.

sections.title: Recursive Binary Search
Lower Bound and Upper Bound Variants
Collections.binarySearch and Arrays.binarySearch
sections.content:
**Java's built-in binary search**:
```java
int[] arr = {1, 3, 5, 7, 9};
int idx = Arrays.binarySearch(arr, 5);   // returns 2
int notFound = Arrays.binarySearch(arr, 4);   // returns -3 (= -(insertionPoint+1))
```

**For lists**:
```java
List<Integer> list = List.of(1, 3, 5, 7, 9);
int idx = Collections.binarySearch(list, 5);   // 2
```

**Return value**:
- If found: index of any match (not guaranteed to be first/last for duplicates).
- If not found: `-(insertion_point) - 1`, where `insertion_point` is where the element would be inserted to keep sorted order.

**Computing insertion point**:
```java
int result = Arrays.binarySearch(arr, target);
int insertionPoint = result >= 0 ? result : -result - 1;
```

**With Comparator**:
```java
int idx = Collections.binarySearch(list, key, comparator);
// or
int idx = Arrays.binarySearch(arr, fromIndex, toIndex, key, comparator);
```

**Important caveats**:
- The list/array MUST be sorted (according to the same comparator/natural order).
- Behavior is undefined on unsorted input — may return any index or -1.
- Doesn't return lower/upper bound for duplicates — just any matching index.
- Time complexity: O(log n) for `RandomAccess` lists (e.g., ArrayList); O(n) for non-random-access (e.g., LinkedList) due to linear traversal to mid.

**Performance tip**: don't use `Collections.binarySearch` on a `LinkedList` — it's O(n) due to traversal cost. Convert to `ArrayList` or use a different data structure (TreeMap).
